newsitem.title: USA: Gateway-Advanced Logic deal positive - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Gateway-Advanced Logic deal positive - analysts.

text.p: Gateway 2000 Inc, known for directly marketing personal computers to individuals, is taking a positive step to expand in the lucrative corporate market through its agreed purchase of Advanced Logic Research Inc.
"I think this looks very attractive and very interesting," said Wendy Abramowitz, an analyst with Argus Research.

Late Thursday, North Sioux City, S.D.-based Gateway said it signed a definitive agreement to buy ALR for $194 million or $15.50 a share. The Irvine, Calif.-based company specializes in computer servers, the high-powered central computers used in corporate and other networks.
Also important, analysts said, is the opportunity for Gateway to increase its product distribution channels.
Gateway said it will continue to sell its brand-name products, with the distinctive cow-spotted boxes, through its own catalogs, its own chain of so-called "country stores" and its Internet Web site.

But the acquisition represents "a great opportunity to broaden the ALR product line with the Gateway product platform," Gateway founder, chairman and chief executive Ted Waitt said in a teleconference with reporters late Thursday.
"Aside from getting directly into the server market, this also expands their channel presence," Abramowitz said.
The main attraction in the deal appears to be ALR's technology for servers, a product line Gateway had been hoping to enter.
"They are doing this less for ALR's revenues. The purpose is to acquire ALR's server technology," said Jay Vleeschhouwer, senior vice president and analyst for Josephthal Lyon & Ross.

Server products tend to have higher margins than consumer PCs, and are essential to landing large corporate accounts. Gateway has said about 36 percent of its annual revenues come from large corporate accounts, a number it has been pushing to increase.
"Without the acquisition Gateway wouldn't have got in (the server market) until late this year or early next," he added.

ALR's $218 million in fiscal 1996 revenues is just four percent of Gateway's $5 billion. And the acquisition price tag is slightly lower than ALR's annual revenues, which analysts agreed is appropriate.
Matthew Russo, an analyst for Sands Brothers & Co, said along with the technology and distribution channels comes ALR's $60 million in cash reported on its balance sheet.
"The purchase price seems very fair...and it will have a positive effect on their bottom line," Russo said.
Waitt said that the deal is expected to immediately begin adding to earnings.

The analysts said the acquisition gives Gateway a better shot at taking on players such as Compaq Computer Corp, which has a large share of the corporate market. Published reports recently said Compaq and Gateway were in talks to merge, but in a conference call with reporters Waitt said, "Gateway is not for sale."
"They decided they didn't want to go ahead with that, and at this point, this will make them more competitive," Argus' Abramowitz said.
On Friday, shares of Gateway traded up 3/4 to 33-7/8 and Advanced Logic was up 1-1/4 at 15-3/8.
